skill.hx.ie.history.title: The infective endocarditis history
skill.hx.ie.history.oneLine: A known valve, a recent portal of entry, and the fever pattern that has been going on longer than it should
skill.hx.ie.history.why: This history is where the diagnosis is usually first suspected, days before any test confirms it. Missing the portal-of-entry question is the single commonest reason the diagnosis is delayed.

asks.text: Do you have a known heart murmur, valve problem, or a prosthetic heart valve?
How has your fever behaved: continuous, or coming and going, with chills or drenching sweats?
Any dental work, tooth extraction, or ongoing dental problems in the last few months?
Do you inject any drugs, or have you had any recent procedure, catheter, piercing or tattoo?
Any weight loss, loss of appetite, or generalised joint and muscle aches?
Any new skin spots, painful lumps on your fingers or toes, or changes in your vision?
Any new weakness, numbness, or difficulty speaking, which could suggest a stroke from an embolus?
Any breathlessness that might suggest the valve itself is now failing?

teach.heading: The portal of entry is a question you must ask, not wait to be told
teach.body: Patients rarely connect a tooth extraction three weeks ago with a fever today. Ask directly about dental work, injecting drug use, and any recent invasive procedure, since finding the portal both supports the diagnosis and identifies what needs addressing afterward.
teach.note: In practice, no portal of entry is found in a substantial proportion of cases, so a negative answer does not argue against the diagnosis; it simply means you did not find one this time.

teach.heading: Read the fever, don't just record it
teach.body: A subacute course, low-grade or intermittent fever over weeks with malaise, weight loss and night sweats, points towards a less virulent organism on an already-damaged valve. A more acute, high, sustained fever with a rapidly unwell patient points towards a more virulent organism, often on a previously normal valve.

pitfalls: Never asking specifically about dental work or intravenous drug use.
Treating a negative portal-of-entry history as evidence against the diagnosis.
Not asking about embolic symptoms (weakness, vision change, abdominal or flank pain) because the presenting complaint was simply 'fever'.

probes.q: Name two classic portals of entry you should always ask about.
probes.a: Dental work or extraction, and intravenous drug use (or another recent invasive procedure or catheter).

probes.q: What fever pattern, together with weeks of malaise and weight loss, suggests a subacute presentation?
probes.a: A low-grade, intermittent fever over an extended period, typically with a less virulent organism on an already-damaged valve.

probes.q: A patient has fever and a known heart murmur but denies any dental work, drug use or recent procedure. Does this make endocarditis unlikely?
probes.a: No. A portal of entry is not identified in a substantial proportion of genuine cases, so its absence does not argue against the diagnosis; the fever and murmur combination still needs to be actively investigated.

rubric.text: Actively asks about dental work, IV drug use and recent procedures
Characterises the fever pattern and its duration
Screens for embolic and immunologic symptoms

skill.exam.ie.stigmata.title: The peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis
skill.exam.ie.stigmata.oneLine: Splinter haemorrhages, Osler's nodes, Janeway lesions and Roth spots, and which mechanism produces each
skill.exam.ie.stigmata.why: These findings are frequently taught as a list to memorise for an exam and then never actually looked for on the ward. Each one is genuinely a bedside sign of active endocarditis, and each is either embolic or immunologic in origin, which is the detail that makes them memorable rather than arbitrary.

steps.text: Examine both hands closely: the fingertip pulps for tender nodules, the nail beds under good light for linear haemorrhages, and the palms for small erythematous macules.
Examine the conjunctivae for petechiae and any subconjunctival haemorrhage.
Perform fundoscopy specifically looking for retinal haemorrhages with a pale centre.
Palpate the abdomen for splenomegaly.
Re-examine the fingers for clubbing, which develops later, in a more prolonged, subacute course.

skill.exam.ie.stigmata.normal: No splinter haemorrhages, no tender nodules on the pulps, no palmar or plantar macules, no conjunctival petechiae, no retinal changes, no splenomegaly, no clubbing.
skill.exam.ie.stigmata.abnormal: Splinter haemorrhages under the nails, tender erythematous nodules on the finger or toe pulps (Osler's nodes), painless erythematous or haemorrhagic macules on the palms or soles (Janeway lesions), retinal haemorrhages with a pale centre (Roth spots), conjunctival petechiae, splenomegaly, or clubbing.
skill.exam.ie.stigmata.significance: Splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions and splenomegaly are embolic phenomena, from tiny fragments of the vegetation lodging distally. Osler's nodes, Roth spots and conjunctival petechiae are immunologic phenomena, from circulating immune complexes depositing in small vessels. Finding any of these in a febrile patient, especially with a known or changing murmur, should move endocarditis to the top of the differential.

teach.heading: Embolic versus immunologic, and why the distinction is worth keeping

rows: Splinter haemorrhages, Janeway lesions, splenomegaly, and, systemically, stroke or renal/splenic infarcts
Osler's nodes, Roth spots, conjunctival petechiae, and glomerulonephritis

teach.note: Osler's nodes are classically described as tender; Janeway lesions are classically described as painless. That single difference, tender versus painless, is the fastest way to tell them apart at the bedside.

teach.heading: Where to actually look

points.d: Splinter haemorrhages under the nail beds, and the finger pulps for Osler's nodes.
Janeway lesions - flat, non-tender, and easy to miss unless you look directly.
Conjunctival petechiae on the lower lid, and fundoscopy for Roth spots if you have an ophthalmoscope.
Dipstick for haematuria, and a fever chart, since the immunologic and embolic signs both sit alongside evidence of the underlying infective process.

teach.note: None of these signs is sensitive on its own. Finding two or more in a febrile patient with a murmur is what should prompt blood cultures and an echocardiogram.

pitfalls: Examining only the hands and skipping fundoscopy and the abdomen.
Confusing Osler's nodes with Janeway lesions; the tender-versus-painless distinction is the key.
Treating the absence of stigmata as evidence against the diagnosis; they are far from universally present, especially early in the illness.
Forgetting that splinter haemorrhages have several non-infective causes, including trauma, and are not specific on their own.

probes.q: Name two peripheral stigmata of infective endocarditis and where you would look for each.
probes.a: Splinter haemorrhages under the nails, and Osler's nodes on the finger or toe pulps (or Janeway lesions on the palms/soles, or Roth spots on fundoscopy).

probes.q: What is the key clinical difference between an Osler's node and a Janeway lesion?
probes.a: Osler's nodes are tender; Janeway lesions are painless.

probes.q: Classify Osler's nodes, Roth spots, splinter haemorrhages and Janeway lesions as embolic or immunologic.
probes.a: Splinter haemorrhages and Janeway lesions are embolic, from vegetation fragments; Osler's nodes and Roth spots are immunologic, from circulating immune complexes.

rubric.text: Examines the hands systematically for nodules and splinter haemorrhages
Performs or documents fundoscopy specifically for Roth spots
Correctly distinguishes Osler's nodes from Janeway lesions

skill.hx.chd.history.title: The congenital heart disease history
skill.hx.chd.history.oneLine: Growth, effort tolerance, cyanotic spells, and the antenatal story
skill.hx.chd.history.why: In a child, growth and effort tolerance carry the diagnostic weight that breathlessness grading carries in an adult, and both parent and child need age-appropriate versions of the same questions. Missing the antenatal history and the family history means missing a clue to an associated syndrome that can point straight at the specific lesion.

asks.text: How has the child's growth been: is weight gain and height tracking normally on the growth chart?
As a baby, did feeding take a long time, or did the baby get tired, sweaty or breathless while feeding?
How is the child's effort tolerance compared to other children the same age: running, playing, keeping up?
Has the child had recurrent chest infections, more than would be expected for age?
Has anyone ever noticed the child turning blue, especially around the lips, or during crying or feeding?
Does the child ever squat down suddenly after exertion?
Was the pregnancy uneventful: any infection (particularly rubella), medication, or maternal illness such as diabetes during it?
Is there any family history of congenital heart disease, or a known genetic syndrome?

teach.heading: Growth is the paediatric equivalent of grading breathlessness
teach.body: A significant left-to-right shunt increases metabolic demand and can cause difficulty feeding in infancy, from breathlessness and fatigue during feeds, leading to poor weight gain. Ask specifically about feeding as an infant, not just current appetite.
teach.note: A well-grown, asymptomatic child with an incidentally found murmur is itself useful evidence that the lesion is small, exactly as normal growth argued for a small VSD in the worked case.

teach.heading: Squatting is a specific clue, not a general one
teach.body: Squatting after exertion is described classically in cyanotic lesions such as tetralogy of Fallot: it increases systemic vascular resistance, which transiently reduces the right-to-left shunt and improves oxygenation. Its presence points away from a simple acyanotic shunt and towards a cyanotic lesion instead.
teach.note: Absence of squatting in an otherwise well child is a genuine negative finding worth documenting, not just a box to tick.

pitfalls: Asking about current appetite instead of feeding difficulty as an infant, which is the more specific historical clue.
Never asking about squatting, cyanotic spells, or antenatal exposures.
Treating an asymptomatic incidental murmur as needing no history at all, when growth and effort tolerance still need to be actively established.

probes.q: Why does poor weight gain matter in an infant with a suspected congenital heart lesion?
probes.a: A significant left-to-right shunt increases metabolic demand and can cause feeding difficulty from breathlessness and fatigue, leading to failure to thrive; poor growth is a genuine marker of a haemodynamically significant lesion.

probes.q: What does squatting after exertion classically suggest?
probes.a: A cyanotic lesion, classically tetralogy of Fallot, since squatting increases systemic vascular resistance and transiently reduces the right-to-left shunt.

probes.q: Why is the antenatal history relevant to a suspected congenital heart lesion?
probes.a: Certain maternal exposures, particularly rubella infection, and certain maternal conditions such as diabetes, are recognised associations with specific congenital heart lesions, so the antenatal history can raise or narrow suspicion before any examination finding.

rubric.text: Establishes growth and infant feeding history
Screens for cyanosis and squatting
Asks about the antenatal and family history

skill.hx.cvs.palpitations.title: Palpitations
skill.hx.cvs.palpitations.oneLine: Fast or slow, regular or irregular, and what the patient felt at the start and the end
skill.hx.cvs.palpitations.why: Palpitation is an awareness of the heartbeat, and the arrhythmia has usually gone by the time you see the patient. The history is often the only recording you will ever get, so it has to be taken as if you were reading a rhythm strip.

asks.text: Tap out on the table what your heart was doing. Ask them to actually do it.
Was it fast or slow, and was it regular or irregular?
Did it start suddenly, like a switch, or build up gradually?
How did it stop: suddenly, or did it fade away?
How long did it last: seconds, minutes, or hours?
What were you doing when it started? Standing up quickly, exertion, or at rest?
Did you pass a lot of urine after the attack settled?
Any blackout, chest pain, breathlessness or severe fatigue with it?
Coffee, alcohol, tobacco, inhalers, thyroid symptoms, or new medicines?

teach.heading: Tapping it out is worth more than any adjective
teach.body: Ask the patient to tap the rhythm. A regular fast tapping, abrupt at both ends, is a paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. An irregularly irregular tapping is atrial fibrillation. A single thump followed by a pause is an ectopic beat and its compensatory pause, which is the commonest and most benign of all.

rows: Sudden on, sudden off, fast and regular
A skipped beat, then a thump
Gradual onset and gradual offset, with anxiety

teach.note: Onset and offset are the most discriminating parts of the history. A switch-like start and stop means a re-entrant circuit.

teach.heading: Post-palpitation diuresis
teach.body: A patient who passes a large volume of urine once the palpitation settles has given you a clue worth having. Atrial stretch during the tachycardia drives natriuretic peptide secretion, and the diuresis follows when the rhythm breaks. It points to an atrial arrhythmia, classically atrial fibrillation.
teach.note: Patients volunteer this rarely and remember it clearly once asked. It costs one question.

teach.heading: The features that make this structural rather than benign

points.d: Stokes-Adams attacks are sudden loss of consciousness from a transient arrest of cerebral perfusion, classically in complete heart block. This is not a benign palpitation.

points.t: Chest pain, breathlessness or severe fatigue with it.
points.d: Suggests underlying structural heart disease rather than an isolated rhythm disturbance.
Raises exercise-induced ventricular arrhythmia, which is dangerous.

points.t: Family history of sudden cardiac death.
points.d: Ask it explicitly. It changes the urgency completely.

teach.heading: Posture and precipitant
teach.body: Palpitations that begin immediately on standing suggest orthostatic intolerance or atrioventricular nodal re-entry. Those tied to anxiety or panic are usually a sinus tachycardia secondary to the mental state, which is a diagnosis of exclusion and not a first assumption. Always ask about caffeine, alcohol, tobacco, inhaled beta agonists and thyroid symptoms.

pitfalls: Recording 'palpitations' without rate, rhythm, onset and offset, which is the whole diagnosis.
Not asking the patient to tap it out, and settling for the word 'fast'.
Missing syncope accompanying the palpitation, which turns a benign symptom into an urgent one.
Attributing it to anxiety before asking about exertion, family history of sudden death, and thyroid symptoms.

probes.q: Sudden onset, sudden offset, fast and regular. What rhythm?
probes.a: A paroxysmal supraventricular tachycardia. The abrupt start and stop reflect a re-entrant circuit beginning and terminating.

probes.q: Why does a patient pass a large volume of urine after an episode of atrial fibrillation settles?
probes.a: Atrial stretch during the tachycardia stimulates natriuretic peptide release, producing a diuresis once the rhythm converts. It points to an atrial arrhythmia.

probes.q: Palpitations with sudden loss of consciousness and rapid full recovery. What is the mechanism and what is the underlying rhythm likely to be?
probes.a: A Stokes-Adams attack: a transient failure of cardiac output, usually from complete heart block or a ventricular arrhythmia, causing abrupt cerebral hypoperfusion. Recovery is rapid and complete once the rhythm resumes, with no post-ictal confusion.

rubric.text: Establishes rate and regularity, ideally by asking the patient to tap it out
Asks about the manner of onset and offset
Asks about post-palpitation diuresis
Screens for syncope, exertional onset and family history of sudden death

skill.hx.cvs.syncope.title: Syncope and blackouts
skill.hx.cvs.syncope.oneLine: Before, during and after, which is what separates cardiac syncope from a seizure and from a faint
skill.hx.cvs.syncope.why: Syncope is a transient loss of consciousness from inadequate cerebral perfusion, with spontaneous recovery and no resuscitation. Roughly a third of people have an episode in their lifetime, and most are benign. The task is finding the cardiac ones, because about a quarter of those go on to a cardiac arrest.

asks.text: What were you doing at the moment it happened: standing, standing up, exerting, or sitting?
Was there any warning: light-headedness, nausea, sweating, tunnel vision?
Ask a witness. How long were you out, and were there any jerking movements?
Were you confused afterwards, or clear-headed straight away?
Any tongue biting, particularly the side, or incontinence?
How many attacks, over what period?
Any palpitation, chest pain or breathlessness just before?
Any family history of sudden death under 40?

teach.heading: Syncope, seizure or a fall: the three-part history
teach.note: Brief jerking during a faint is common and does NOT make it a seizure. Post-event confusion and a lateral tongue bite are what point to a seizure.

teach.heading: The circumstance names the mechanism

points.d: Orthostatic hypotension. Ask about diuretics, antihypertensives, alpha blockers, dehydration and autonomic neuropathy.

points.t: Prolonged standing, heat, pain, the sight of blood, venepuncture.
points.d: Classical vasovagal syncope, with a clear prodrome.
The dangerous one: aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or an exercise-induced arrhythmia. Syncope on exertion is cardiac until proven otherwise.
More often vasovagal, but does not exclude a cardiac cause.

points.t: On turning the head or with a tight collar.
points.d: Carotid sinus hypersensitivity.
Situational syncope.

teach.heading: What makes it cardiac, and therefore urgent
teach.body: No prodrome, occurring while sitting or lying, occurring during exertion, preceded by palpitation, or in a patient with known structural heart disease or a family history of sudden death under 40. Any one of these moves the patient from reassurance to investigation.
teach.note: Presyncope carries the same significance as syncope. A patient who nearly blacked out on exertion needs the same workup as one who did.

pitfalls: Taking the history only from the patient, when the useful part is what the witness saw.
Calling brief jerking a seizure, and missing a cardiac cause.
Not separating syncope ON exertion from syncope AFTER exertion.
Dismissing presyncope as less important than a completed blackout.

probes.q: Which single feature most strongly suggests a seizure rather than a faint?
probes.a: Prolonged post-event confusion, along with a lateral tongue bite. Brief jerking alone occurs in faints too.

probes.q: Why is syncope occurring DURING exertion so much more worrying than syncope after it?
probes.a: During exertion the demand for cardiac output is highest, so syncope implies a fixed obstruction such as aortic stenosis or hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, or an exercise-induced arrhythmia. Post-exertional syncope is more often vasovagal, as venous return falls when the muscle pump stops.

probes.q: A patient blacks out while seated, with no warning, and recovers fully within seconds. Why does the absence of a prodrome point to a cardiac cause?
probes.a: A vasovagal faint develops over seconds through autonomic activation, which produces nausea, sweating and visual dimming. An abrupt arrhythmic loss of cardiac output gives no time for any prodrome, so consciousness is lost without warning and returns as soon as the rhythm recovers.

rubric.text: Establishes posture and activity at the moment of the event
Asks about warning symptoms
Seeks a witness account of duration and movements
Distinguishes immediate recovery from post-event confusion
Screens for exertional onset, palpitation and family history of sudden death

skill.hx.cvs.treatment.title: The treatment history, and what it tells you
skill.hx.cvs.treatment.oneLine: The schedule of a drug often names the diagnosis before the patient does
skill.hx.cvs.treatment.why: Patients frequently cannot name their medicines but can describe how they take them. A dosing schedule, a monitoring blood test, or an injection interval is often enough to infer the diagnosis, and it is information no investigation will give you.

asks.text: Bring me everything you take, including the strips and the old prescriptions.
How often do you take each one? Every day, or only on certain days?
Do you have a regular blood test for any of them? Which one, and how often?
Do you get any injections? How often, and where do you get them?
How long have you been on each, and has anything been stopped recently?
Have you missed any doses in the last week? Ask how many, not whether.

teach.heading: Read the schedule, infer the diagnosis
teach.body: A patient who says only that they take 'a heart tablet' has still told you a great deal if you ask how and when.

rows: Taken five days a week, with a gap
A regular blood test to adjust the dose
A metallic valve, atrial fibrillation or venous thrombosis
An intramuscular injection once every three weeks
Rheumatic heart disease, on secondary prophylaxis
A tablet under the tongue for chest pain
A water tablet, with the dose doubled on bad days
Heart failure with a self-adjusted regimen

teach.note: The three-weekly injection is the one most often missed, and it establishes rheumatic heart disease and adherence to prophylaxis in a single question.

teach.heading: Adherence, asked in a way that gets an honest answer
teach.body: Do not ask whether the patient is compliant, because the answer is always yes. Ask how many doses they missed in the last week, and ask what they do when they run out or cannot afford the next strip. Cost and supply are among the commonest reasons for decompensation and are almost never volunteered.

teach.heading: What was stopped, and when
teach.body: A recently stopped beta blocker, a diuretic held for a procedure, or an anticoagulant interrupted for dental work can each explain the presentation in front of you. Ask specifically about anything stopped in the last month, and who stopped it.

pitfalls: Accepting 'some heart tablets' and moving on, when the schedule would have named them.
Not asking about injections, and missing benzathine penicillin prophylaxis.
Not asking about monitoring blood tests, and missing warfarin.
Asking whether the patient is compliant instead of how many doses were missed.
Failing to ask what was stopped recently, which often explains the admission.

probes.q: A patient has an intramuscular injection once every three weeks. What is it, and what does it imply?
probes.a: Benzathine penicillin for secondary prophylaxis of rheumatic fever, which implies established rheumatic heart disease.

probes.q: A patient reports a regular blood test to adjust one of their tablets. Which drug, and what should you ask next?
probes.a: Warfarin, monitored by INR. Ask the target range, the most recent value, and the indication: a metallic valve, atrial fibrillation, or venous thromboembolism.

probes.q: Why does a drug taken five days a week rather than daily suggest digoxin, and what must you check before increasing any cardiac drug in that patient?
probes.a: Digoxin has a narrow therapeutic index and a long half life, so drug-free days were a traditional way to limit accumulation. Before changing anything, check renal function and potassium, since both alter digoxin toxicity, and ask about nausea, visual disturbance and confusion.

rubric.text: Obtains an actual inventory rather than a recollection
Uses schedule, monitoring and injections to infer the drug
Asks adherence in a way that permits an honest answer
Asks what was stopped recently, and by whom

skill.annex.defs.cvs.title: Definitions: the hypertension family
skill.annex.defs.cvs.oneLine: Resistant, refractory, pseudoresistant, masked and white coat are five different problems
skill.annex.defs.cvs.why: A patient whose blood pressure will not come down is not automatically resistant hypertension. Most are pseudoresistant, and the management of each of these five is completely different, so the label decides what happens next.

teach.heading: Five labels, five different next steps

rows: Above target despite three drugs at optimal dose, one of them a diuretic
Confirm adherence, then screen for secondary causes
Above target despite five or more drugs including a diuretic and a mineralocorticoid antagonist
Specialist referral; a much smaller group
Appears resistant, but from poor technique, poor adherence, or white coat effect
Fix the measurement and the adherence FIRST
Raised in clinic, normal outside it
Confirm with ambulatory or home readings
Normal in clinic, raised outside it
The dangerous one, because it is missed

teach.note: Pseudoresistance is the commonest of these by a wide margin. Wrong cuff size, an unrested patient, and unreported non-adherence explain more apparent resistance than any endocrine cause.

teach.heading: Emergency, urgency and malignant

points.d: Severe hypertension WITH acute target organ damage: encephalopathy, pulmonary oedema, dissection, acute kidney injury, eclampsia. The organ damage defines it, not the number.
Severe hypertension WITHOUT acute organ damage. Lowered over days with oral therapy, not acutely.
Severe hypertension with retinal haemorrhages, exudates or papilloedema, and often renal impairment.

teach.note: The distinction between emergency and urgency is made by examining the patient, most usefully the fundi, not by the height of the reading.

teach.heading: Pseudohypertension
teach.body: In heavily calcified, incompressible arteries the cuff must be inflated well above true intra-arterial pressure to occlude the vessel, so the recorded pressure is falsely high. Suspect it in an elderly patient with very high readings, few end-organ changes, and symptoms of over-treatment such as dizziness on standing.

pitfalls: Labelling a patient resistant before excluding poor technique and non-adherence.
Deciding emergency versus urgency from the number rather than from target organ assessment.
Missing masked hypertension because clinic readings are normal and nobody measures outside.
Escalating drugs in an elderly patient with pseudohypertension, causing postural symptoms.

probes.q: What separates a hypertensive emergency from an urgency?
probes.a: Acute target organ damage. The emergency has it; the urgency does not. The blood pressure reading itself does not decide.

probes.q: Why is masked hypertension more dangerous than white coat hypertension?
probes.a: Because it is missed. The clinic reading is normal, so the patient is never treated, while the pressure is genuinely raised for most of the day and organ damage accumulates.

probes.q: An 80 year old has readings of 200/110, no retinopathy, no left ventricular hypertrophy, and becomes dizzy on treatment. What should be suspected and why?
probes.a: Pseudohypertension. Calcified, incompressible arteries need cuff pressures far above the true intra-arterial pressure to occlude, so the recorded value overstates reality. Treating to the recorded number then produces genuine hypotension.

rubric.text: Excludes pseudoresistance before labelling resistance
Separates emergency from urgency by target organ damage
Considers masked hypertension when clinic readings are normal
